**The Weight of Silence**

The first time I understood the weight of silence, I was twelve years old, sitting on the edge of my bed with a half-eaten sandwich in my lap and a comic book I couldn’t focus on. My father had just left the room after another one of his long, quiet stares—the kind that made the air thick enough to choke on. He didn’t yell. He didn’t slam doors. He just… existed in a way that felt like a storm holding back.

That night, I learned two things: silence could be louder than screams, and some wounds don’t bleed—they fester.

---

**The House on Willow Street**

The house on Willow Street was painted the color of wet slate, its shutters peeling like old skin. I bought it on a whim, or maybe on a dare, because the realtor’s smile had been too polished and his eyes had darted to the back yard—where the old oak tree stood, its branches twisted like arthritic fingers. The previous owner had died there, they said. Not violently. Not suddenly. Just… gone, one morning, leaving behind a kitchen table set for three and a half-finished cup of tea.

I moved in with a suitcase and a cat named Miso. The first night, I woke to the sound of something scratching at the back door. Not an animal. Not the wind. A slow, deliberate *tap-tap-tap*, like fingernails on wood. I told myself it was the house settling. But the next morning, the doorknob was warm to the touch, as if someone had been leaning against it from the outside.

I never found out who lived there before me. Some things are better left unanswered.

---

**The Last Letter**

My grandmother’s letters were yellowed at the edges, the ink faded like old bruises. She wrote them in the 1950s, when she was young and the world was still full of possibilities. She never sent them. She just folded them carefully and tucked them into a shoebox under her bed.

I found them when I was cleaning out her apartment after she passed. The first one was to her mother, who had disowned her for marrying a man her family didn’t approve of. The second was to her first love, a soldier who never came back from the war. The last one was to me, though she never got the chance to write it.

I read them all in one sitting, the weight of her unspoken words pressing down on me like a tombstone. Some letters are meant to be burned. Others are meant to be kept, like secrets that refuse to stay buried.

---

**The Man Who Collected Tears**

There was a man in my hometown who claimed he could collect tears. Not in jars or bottles—he said they had to be fresh, still warm on the skin. He’d stand outside the funeral home, the hospital, the courthouse, offering a handkerchief to anyone who needed to cry. And when they did, he’d press the cloth to their face, then slip it into a small velvet pouch.

People said he was a fraud. Others whispered he was a saint. I never asked. But one day, I saw him kneeling in the alley behind the diner, his head bowed over a crumpled napkin. He was crying too.

I walked away before he could see me. Some things aren’t meant to be witnessed.

---

**The Girl Who Spoke in Reverse**

Lena was the only person I knew who spoke in reverse. Not backwards—*reverse*. She’d say things like, *"I see you, you see me"* instead of *"You see me, I see you."* It wasn’t a trick. It wasn’t a game. It was just how her mind worked.

I met her at a café when I was twenty, and we talked for hours. She told me about her childhood, about how her parents had taken her to a linguist when she was five because they thought she was "confused." The linguist had just smiled and said, *"She’s not confused. She’s speaking in a language we’ve forgotten how to understand."*

Lena disappeared a year later. No one knew where she went. Some said she’d found a place where people spoke like her. Others said she’d finally learned to speak the way the rest of us did.

I still think about her sometimes, wondering if she ever found her way home.

---

**The Clock That Ran Backward**

My grandfather’s pocket watch was broken. Not in the way that timepieces usually break—it didn’t stop. It didn’t tick erratically. It ran *backward*.

He gave it to me on his deathbed, his hands shaking as he pressed it into my palm. *"Wind it up,"* he rasped. *"But don’t look at the time."*

I did. Of course I did.

The hands spun counterclockwise, the seconds unraveling like thread. I wound it up every morning, just to see. Sometimes, when I wasn’t looking, it would stop. And when I checked again, the time would be exactly where it had been the last time I’d seen it.

I still have the watch. I don’t wear it. But sometimes, when I’m alone, I take it out and listen to the way it ticks—*tick-tock, tick-tock*—like it’s counting down to something I’ll never understand.

---

**The Bridge at Midnight**

There’s a bridge in my city that’s only open at midnight. No one knows why. The city records say it was built in the 1920s, but no one remembers the original purpose. Some say it’s a shortcut to another part of town. Others say it’s a shortcut to nowhere at all.

I walked across it once, just after midnight, the streetlights flickering like dying fireflies. The air smelled like rain and old metal. Halfway across, I heard footsteps behind me—slow, deliberate, like someone dragging their feet. I turned, but there was no one there.

When I reached the other side, the bridge was gone. No trace of it remained, as if it had never been there.

I’ve never gone back. Some doors shouldn’t be opened twice.

---

**The Last Laugh**

My uncle was a comedian. Not the kind who made people laugh—he made them *uncomfortable*. His jokes were sharp, like broken glass, and his timing was off in a way that made you wonder if he was trying to hurt you or just didn’t care.

The night he died, he was on stage, telling a joke about a man who laughed so hard he cried, and then cried so hard he laughed, and then—

He just stopped. Mid-sentence. His face went slack, his eyes rolled back, and he collapsed onto the mic stand. The audience thought it was part of the act. No one realized he was dead until the paramedics arrived.

His last words were never spoken. But I like to think he got the last laugh after all.

---

**The Weight of Words**

Words are strange things. They can build or destroy, heal or wound. They can be whispered in the dark or shouted from rooftops. They can be written in ink or carved into stone.

But some words are heavier than others. They sit in your chest like a stone, pressing down until you can’t breathe. They’re the words you wish you could take back. The words you wish you’d never heard.

I’ve carried a few of those in my life. Some belong to others. Some belong to me.

And every now and then, I wonder if there’s a way to let them go.

---

**The End (Or Maybe the Beginning)**

I don’t know where this ends. Maybe it doesn’t. Maybe it’s just a collection of moments, like loose change in a pocket—some shiny, some tarnished, all waiting to be spent.

I could keep writing. There are more stories. More ghosts. More unanswered questions.

But for now, I’ll leave it here.

Because some things are better left unsaid.

And some things are better left to the silence.
